title: nth Roots: Points on a Circle

steps.body: Run De Moivre backwards to take roots. A number r(cos θ + i sin θ) has exactly **n distinct nth roots**, all with modulus **r^(1/n)** and arguments **(θ + 2πk)/n** for k = 0, 1, …, n−1. They sit on a circle, **equally spaced** 2π/n apart — a perfect n-gon.

widget.prompt: Every cube root of 8 shares the same modulus. Slide the base until base^(1/3) reads 2.
widget.successFeedback: 8^(1/3) = 2 — and that is the modulus every one of the three cube roots shares, however different their angles are. Roots of a complex number fan out around a circle of exactly this radius; only the angle changes between them.

explanationVariants: Three cube roots, spaced 2π/3 = 120° apart around the circle of radius 2.
n = 3 roots form an equilateral triangle; spacing 360°/3 = 120°.

widget.prompt: The three cube roots of 8 are spaced how far apart?

options.label: 120° (2π/3)
options.feedback: Right — n roots divide the full turn evenly: 360°/3 = 120°.
90° would be for FOUR roots (360/4). Cube roots (n = 3) are 120° apart.
That's a full turn — all three fit INSIDE it, one every 120°.

explanationVariants: k = 0 gives argument 0: the root is 2(cos 0 + i sin 0) = 2, the obvious real cube root.
The first root (k = 0) sits on the positive real axis at 2.

widget.prompt: Which is one of the cube roots of 8?

options.label: 2, the real cube root of 8 when k = 0.
options.feedback: Right — modulus 2, argument 0: the real cube root, since 2³ = 8.

options.label: 8, the original value rather than a cube root.
options.feedback: 8 is the number, not a root: 8³ = 512 ≠ 8. The real root is 2.

options.label: 4, whose cube is 64 rather than 8.
options.feedback: 4³ = 64 ≠ 8. The real cube root has modulus 8^(1/3) = 2.

steps.body: The **roots of unity** are the nth roots of 1: modulus 1, arguments 2πk/n — n points evenly spaced on the unit circle, always including 1 itself. The fourth roots of 1 are 1, i, −1, −i: a square inscribed in the unit circle.

explanationVariants: The 4th roots of 1 have modulus 1 and arguments 0, 90°, 180°, 270° — namely 1, i, −1, −i, the corners of a square.
i is one such root: i⁴ = (i²)² = 1.

widget.prompt: Which is a fourth root of 1?

options.label: i
options.feedback: Right — i⁴ = (i²)² = (−1)² = 1, and i sits at 90° on the unit circle.
2⁴ = 16 ≠ 1. All roots of unity have modulus 1, so 2 is too far out.

options.label: 1 + i
options.feedback: |1 + i| = √2 ≠ 1, so it's off the unit circle. The roots are 1, i, −1, −i.

explanationVariants: i has modulus 1, argument π/2. Its two square roots have modulus 1 and arguments (π/2)/2 = π/4 and (π/2 + 2π)/2 = 5π/4. The k = 0 root is cos 45° + i sin 45° = (√2/2)(1 + i) ≈ 0.7071 + 0.7071i; its real part is √2/2 ≈ 0.7071.
The principal square root of i sits at 45°: real part cos 45° = √2/2 ≈ 0.7071.
hints: Write i in polar form: modulus 1, argument π/2.
The k = 0 root is at π/4; its real part is cos(π/4).

widget.prompt: The principal (k = 0) square root of i has what real part? (To four decimals.)

commonErrors.feedback: 0.5 = cos 60°. The root's angle is π/4 (45°), so the real part is cos 45° = √2/2 ≈ 0.7071.
cos of the root angle π/4 is √2/2 ≈ 0.7071, not 1 (that would be angle 0).

takeaways: n nth-roots: modulus r^(1/n), arguments (θ + 2πk)/n, spaced 2π/n.
Roots of unity are n evenly spaced points on the unit circle, including 1.
Equal spacing means the roots are the vertices of a regular n-gon.
steps.teaser: Next chapter: parametric equations — curves traced by a moving point over time.

concept.body: nth roots of r(cosθ+isinθ): n of them, modulus r^(1/n), arguments (θ+2πk)/n for k=0..n−1, equally spaced 2π/n around a circle.

explanationVariants: A number has exactly n distinct nth roots — so 5 fifth roots.

widget.prompt: How many distinct fifth roots does a nonzero complex number have?

commonErrors.feedback: Over the complex numbers there are exactly n = 5 fifth roots, not just one.
n distinct roots for the nth root: 5, not 10.
